To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the flow stress of LM-1 increases by a factor of 2.5 as strain-rate increases from 104 to 105/s.
the mechanical behavior of bulk metallic glass LM-1 is strain-rate dependent in the range of 102–106/s, and that the strain-rate dependence can be modeled with a Johnson–Cook constitutive model.
the mechanical properties of Zr41,25Ti13,75Cu12,5Ni10Be2,25 bulk metallic glass were characterized under dynamic strain rates of 102–106 s–1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanical properties of a Zr-based metallic glass under dynamic loading conditions.
the effect of high strain rates, on the mechanical behavior of a Zr-based BMG.
the mechanical behavior of bulk metallic glasses under high strain-rate conditions, and the effect of high strain rates (up to 105/s) on the flow stress and fracture behavior of a Zr-based BMG.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the flow stress and strain hardening behavior of the Zr-based bulk glass is independent of the strain-rate regime.
the flow stress of the bulk metallic glass is independent of the strain rate in the range of 102–104 s−1, and that the flow stress increases by a factor of 2 at a strain rate of 105 s−1.
the mechanical behavior of Zirconium-based bulk metallic glass (BMG) is not significantly affected by the strain rate over the strain rate range of 102–104/s.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mechanical behavior of bulk metallic glasses under high-strain-rate loading can be described by a combination of the quasistatic constitutive response, the strain rate sensitivity, and a dynamic failure criterion.
the mechanical properties of Zr-based bulk-metallic glasses are highly dependent upon the loading conditions.
we have demonstrated the use of a tapered insert in SHPB experiments and have shown that this insert mitigates the effects of stress concentration at the specimen-insert interfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flow stress in the high strain rate plate-impact experiments (≈1.8 Gpa) is higher than in the SHPB tests (≈1 GPa).
the peak stress of a Zr-based metallic glass is strain-rate dependent, and it is possible to achieve a peak stress of ~2 GPa at a strain rate of ~105/s.
the peak stress increases with increasing strain rate, but the increase is not as large as predicted by a rate-sensitive constitutive law that is based on quasistatic data.
